# fpp3 9.11, Ex11

> Choose one of the following seasonal time series: the Australian production of electricity, cement, or gas (from `aus_production`).
>
> a. Do the data need transforming?
>    If so, find a suitable transformation.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
aus_production |>
  autoplot(Electricity)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex11a-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Yes, these need transforming, as the seasonal variation increases with the level of the series.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lambda <- aus_production |>
  features(Electricity, guerrero) |>
  pull(lambda_guerrero)
aus_production |>
  autoplot(box_cox(Electricity, lambda))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex11a2-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The Guerrero method suggests using a Box-Cox transformation with parameter $\lambda = 0.52$.

> b. Are the data stationary?
>    If not, find an appropriate differencing which yields stationary data.

The trend and seasonality show that the data are not stationary.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
aus_production |>
  gg_tsdisplay(
    box_cox(Electricity, lambda) |> difference(4),
    plot_type = "partial"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex11b-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
aus_production |>
  gg_tsdisplay(
    box_cox(Electricity, lambda) |> difference(4) |> difference(1),
    plot_type = "partial"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex11b-2.png){width=672}
:::
:::


- The seasonally differenced data still wander a little, although we could have continued with only taking seasonal differences (you may try this option).
- We take a first order difference as well.

> c. Identify a couple of ARIMA models that might be useful in describing the time series.
>    Which of your models is the best according to their AIC values?

From the above graph, an AR(1) or an MA(1) with a seasonal MA(2) might work.
So we try an ARIMA(1,1,0)(0,1,2)$_4$ model for the transformed data, along with the model chosen by `ARIMA()`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit <- aus_production |>
  model(
    manual = ARIMA(
      box_cox(Electricity, lambda) ~ 0 + pdq(1, 1, 0) + PDQ(0, 1, 2)
    ),
    auto = ARIMA(box_cox(Electricity, lambda))
  )
fit |>
  select(auto) |>
  report()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Series: Electricity 
Model: ARIMA(1,1,4)(0,1,1)[4] 
Transformation: box_cox(Electricity, lambda) 

Coefficients:
          ar1     ma1      ma2      ma3      ma4     sma1
      -0.7030  0.2430  -0.4477  -0.1553  -0.2452  -0.5574
s.e.   0.1739  0.1943   0.0973   0.0931   0.1189   0.1087

sigma^2 estimated as 18.02:  log likelihood=-609.08
AIC=1232.17   AICc=1232.71   BIC=1255.7
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
glance(fit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

1 manual   19.7   -620. 1247. 1248. 1261. <cpl [1]> <cpl [8]>
2 auto     18.0   -609. 1232. 1233. 1256. <cpl [1]> <cpl [8]>
```


:::
:::


Automatic model selection with `ARIMA()` has also taken a first order difference and a seasonal difference, and so we can compare the AIC (or AICc) values.
This is a challenging ARIMA model to select manually and the automatic model is clearly better than mine.

> d. Estimate the parameters of your best model and do diagnostic testing on the residuals.
>    Do the residuals resemble white noise?
>    If not, try to find another ARIMA model which fits better.

The automatic model has 6 parameters, so we use `dof = 6` in the Ljung-Box test.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
  select(auto) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

> e. Forecast the next 24 months of data using your preferred model.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit |>
  select(auto) |>
  forecast(h = "2 years") |>
  autoplot(aus_production)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex11e-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


> f. Compare the forecasts obtained using `ETS()`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
aus_production |>
  model(ETS(Electricity)) |>
  forecast(h = "2 years") |>
  autoplot(aus_production)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex11f-1.png){width=672}

```{.r .cell-code}
aus_production |>
  model(ETS(Electricity)) |>
  forecast(h = "2 years") |>
  autoplot(aus_production |> filter(year(Quarter) >= 2000)) +
  autolayer(
    fit |> select(auto) |> forecast(h = "2 years"),

    alpha = 0.4
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex11f-2.png){width=672}

- The point forecasts appear to be quite similar.
- The ETS forecasts have a wider forecast interval than the ARIMA forecasts.

# fpp3 9.11, Ex12

> For the same time series you used in the previous exercise, try using a non-seasonal model applied to the seasonally adjusted data obtained from STL.
> Compare the forecasts with those obtained in the previous exercise.
> Which do you think is the best approach?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lambda <- aus_production |>
  features(Electricity, guerrero) |>
  pull(lambda_guerrero)
stlarima <- decomposition_model(
  STL(box_cox(Electricity, lambda)),
  ARIMA(season_adjust)
)
fc <- aus_production |>
  model(
    ets = ETS(Electricity),
    arima = ARIMA(box_cox(Electricity, lambda)),
    stlarima = stlarima
  ) |>
  forecast(h = "2 years")
fc |> autoplot(aus_production |> filter(year(Quarter) > 2000), level = 95)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex12-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The STL-ARIMA approach has higher point forecasts (except in the first two quarters).
Its prediction intervals are narrower than those from ETS, but are only narrower than those from ARIMA for the first two quarters.
To decide which approach is best, we compare them on a test set consisting of the last two years of data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
train <- aus_production |>
  filter(Quarter <= max(Quarter) - 8)
fc <- train |>
  model(
    ets = ETS(Electricity),
    arima = ARIMA(box_cox(Electricity, lambda)),
    stlarima = stlarima
  ) |>
  forecast(h = "2 years")
fc |>
  accuracy(
    aus_production,
    list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE, MAPE = MAPE, winkler = winkler_score),
    level = 95
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 6
  .model   .type  RMSE   MAE  MAPE winkler
  <chr>    <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 arima    Test  2550. 2398.  4.04  25547.
2 ets      Test  1978. 1653.  2.76  14472.
3 stlarima Test  2854. 2644.  4.46  32339.
```


:::
:::


On this test set, ETS is best on all measures, followed by the seasonal ARIMA model, with the STL-ARIMA approach the worst.
The Winkler scores show that the narrower prediction intervals from the ARIMA and STL-ARIMA models are too narrow, rather than more precise.
One test set of eight quarters is not much evidence, but I would use the ETS model here.

# fpp3 9.11, Ex13

> For the Australian tourism data (from `tourism`):
>
> a. Fit ARIMA models for each time series.
> b. Produce forecasts of your fitted models.
> c. Check the forecasts for the "Snowy Mountains" and "Melbourne" regions.
>    Do they look reasonable?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit <- tourism |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(Trips))
fc <- fit |> forecast(h = "3 years")
fc |>
  filter(Region == "Snowy Mountains") |>
  autoplot(tourism)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex13-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
fc |>
  filter(Region == "Melbourne") |>
  autoplot(tourism)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex13-2.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Both sets of forecasts appear to have captured the underlying trend and seasonality effectively.
The strong seasonality of holiday travel to the Snowy Mountains is reproduced in the forecasts, while the other Snowy Mountains series have no clear trend or seasonality, so their forecasts are flat.
All four Melbourne series have increased in recent years, and their forecasts continue the upward trends.
One problem is that the lower prediction interval limits for business and other travel to the Snowy Mountains are negative, which is impossible; a log transformation would avoid this.

# fpp3 9.11, Ex14

> For your retail time series (Exercise 5 above):
>
> a. develop an appropriate seasonal ARIMA model;


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(12345678)
myseries <- aus_retail |>
  filter(
    `Series ID` == sample(aus_retail$`Series ID`, 1),
    Month < yearmonth("2018 Jan")
  )
myseries |>
  gg_tsdisplay(log(Turnover) |> difference(lag = 12), plot_type = "partial")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex14a-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


In Exercise 5, we found that logs and a seasonal difference were needed, possibly with a first difference as well.
The ACF of the seasonally differenced data decays slowly, while the PACF has large spikes at lags 1 and 2, suggesting a non-seasonal AR(2) component.
The PACF also has significant spikes at lags 12 and 24, suggesting a seasonal AR(2) component.
So an ARIMA(2,0,0)(2,1,0)$_{12}$ model is a reasonable starting point.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit <- myseries |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(Turnover)))
report(fit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Series: Turnover 
Model: ARIMA(2,0,1)(2,1,1)[12] 
Transformation: log(Turnover) 

Coefficients:
         ar1     ar2      ma1    sar1    sar2     sma1
      0.8867  0.1014  -0.2998  0.1169  0.0170  -0.8573
s.e.  0.0233  0.0244   0.2391  0.0123  0.0321   0.0529

sigma^2 estimated as 0.004729:  log likelihood=430.17
AIC=-846.34   AICc=-846.01   BIC=-819.44
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
gg_tsresiduals(fit)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/ex14a2-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
fit |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  State              Industry                                     .model lb_stat lb_pvalue
  <chr>              <chr>                                        <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Northern Territory Clothing, footwear and personal accessory r… arima     21.5     0.253
```


:::
:::


`ARIMA()` has chosen the same differencing and AR orders, but has also added non-seasonal and seasonal MA(1) terms.
The AR coefficients sum to 0.99, so the model is close to having a unit root, and is similar to a model with a first difference as well as a seasonal difference.
The residuals look like white noise: there are a couple of small spikes in the ACF, but the Ljung-Box test is not significant.

> b. compare the forecasts with those you obtained in earlier chapters;


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
stlets <- decomposition_model(
  STL(log(Turnover)),
  ETS(season_adjust)
)
stlarima <- decomposition_model(
  STL(log(Turnover)),
  ARIMA(season_adjust)
)
fit <- myseries |>
  model(
    ets = ETS(Turnover),
    arima = ARIMA(log(Turnover)),
    stlets = stlets,
    stlarima = stlarima
  )
fc <- fit |>
  forecast(h = "3 years")
fc |>
  accuracy(aus_retail) |>
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  .model    RMSE   MAE
  <chr>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 arima    0.798 0.677
2 ets      0.967 0.777
3 stlarima 0.641 0.487
4 stlets   1.14  0.838
```


:::
:::


From these 4 models, the STL-ARIMA model is doing better than the others.

> c. Obtain up-to-date retail data from the [ABS website](https://bit.ly/absretail) (Cat 8501.0, Table 11), and compare your forecasts with the actual numbers.
>    How good were the forecasts from the various models?

The ABS stopped publishing the Retail Trade series after the June 2025 release, and in that release the Northern Territory clothing series (A3349767W) ends in September 2021. The data below are from Table 11 of that release, for January 2018 -- September 2021.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# ABS Retail Trade, Australia, June 2025, Table 11, Series A3349767W
update <- tsibble(
  Month = yearmonth("2018 Jan") + 0:44,
  Turnover = c(
    11.9, 10.5, 11.6, 12.7, 14.3, 15.3, 16.5, 16.0, 14.3, 14.3, 15.2, 20.1,
    11.7, 10.4, 11.9, 12.3, 13.6, 14.2, 15.5, 15.4, 13.4, 13.5, 14.5, 20.1,
    11.1, 9.8, 9.1, 5.4, 11.8, 14.0, 18.6, 16.4, 15.9, 16.4, 16.7, 25.7,
    13.5, 11.3, 13.6, 14.8, 15.7, 14.9, 16.5, 15.9, 17.4
  ),
  index = Month
)
fc |>
  accuracy(update)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

  .model   .type     ME  RMSE   MAE     MPE  MAPE  MASE RMSSE  ACF1

1 arima    Test  -1.01   1.95  1.40 -10.7   12.7    NaN   NaN 0.568
2 ets      Test  -1.42   2.17  1.60 -13.5   14.3    NaN   NaN 0.564
```

# fpp3 9.11, Ex15

> Consider the number of Snowshoe Hare furs traded by the Hudson Bay Company between 1845 and 1935 (data set `pelt`).
>
> a. Produce a time plot of the time series.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pelt |>
  autoplot(Hare)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


> b. Assume you decide to fit the following model:
>    $$
>      y_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2}
>            + \phi_3 y_{t-3} + \phi_4 y_{t-4} + \varepsilon_t,
>    $$
>    where $\varepsilon_t$ is a white noise series.
>    What sort of ARIMA model is this (i.e., what are $p$, $d$, and $q$)?

- This is an ARIMA(4,0,0), hence $p = 4$, $d = 0$ and $q = 0$.

> c. By examining the ACF and PACF of the data, explain why this model is appropriate.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pelt |> gg_tsdisplay(Hare, plot_type = "partial")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
fit <- pelt |> model(AR4 = ARIMA(Hare ~ pdq(4, 0, 0)))
fit |> gg_tsresiduals()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-2.png){width=672}
:::
:::


- The PACF has significant spikes at lags 1, 2 and 4 (and almost at lag 3), and no significant partial autocorrelations after lag 4, which indicates an AR(4).
- The ACF shows a damped sinusoidal pattern, consistent with an AR model.
- The residuals from this model look like white noise.

> d. The last five values of the series are given below:


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Year                 |  1931|  1932|  1933|  1934|  1935|
|:--------------------|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|
|Number of hare pelts | 19520| 82110| 89760| 81660| 15760|


:::
:::


> The estimated parameters are $c = 30993$, $\phi_1 = 0.82$, $\phi_2 = -0.29$, $\phi_3 = -0.01$, and $\phi_4 = -0.22$.
> Without using the `forecast()` function, calculate forecasts for the next three years (1936--1939).

\begin{align*}
  \hat{y}_{T+1|T} & = 30993 +
    0.82* 15760
    -0.29* 81660
    -0.01* 89760
    -0.22* 82110 =
    2051.57 \\
  \hat{y}_{T+2|T} & = 30993 +
    0.82* 2051.57
    -0.29* 15760
    -0.01* 81660
    -0.22* 89760 =
    8223.14 \\
  \hat{y}_{T+3|T} & = 30993 +
    0.82* 8223.14
    -0.29* 2051.57
    -0.01* 15760
    -0.22* 81660 =
    19387.96 \\
\end{align*}

> e. Now fit the model in R and obtain the forecasts using `forecast()`.
>    How are they different from yours?
>    Why?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pelt |>
  model(ARIMA(Hare ~ pdq(4, 0, 0))) |>
  forecast(h = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A fable: 3 x 4 [1Y]
# Key:     .model [1]
  .model     Year              Hare  .mean
  <chr>     <dbl>            <dist>  <dbl>
1 ARIMA(Ha…  1936  N(2052, 5.9e+08)  2052.
2 ARIMA(Ha…  1937  N(8223, 9.8e+08)  8223.
3 ARIMA(Ha…  1938 N(19388, 1.1e+09) 19388.
```


:::
:::


Any differences will be due to rounding errors.

# fpp3 9.11, Ex16

> The population of Switzerland from 1960 to 2017 is in data set `global_economy`.

> a. Produce a time plot of the data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
swiss_pop <- global_economy |>
  filter(Country == "Switzerland") |>
  select(Year, Population) |>
  mutate(Population = Population / 1e6)

autoplot(swiss_pop, Population)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


> b. You decide to fit the following model to the series:
>    $$
>      y_t = c + y_{t-1} + \phi_1 (y_{t-1} - y_{t-2}) + \phi_2 (y_{t-2} - y_{t-3})
>            + \phi_3( y_{t-3} - y_{t-4}) + \varepsilon_t
>    $$
>    where $y_t$ is the Population in year $t$ and $\varepsilon_t$ is a white noise series.
>    What sort of ARIMA model is this (i.e., what are $p$, $d$, and $q$)?

This is an ARIMA(3,1,0), hence $p = 3$, $d = 1$ and $q = 0$.

> c. Explain why this model was chosen using the ACF and PACF of the differenced series.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
swiss_pop |> gg_tsdisplay(Population, plot_type = "partial")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
swiss_pop |> gg_tsdisplay(difference(Population), plot_type = "partial")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](ex10-sol_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The original series is clearly non-stationary (with a slowly decaying ACF), so it needs differencing.
For the differenced series, the last significant spike in the PACF is at lag 3, and the ACF decays in a damped sinusoidal pattern, which signals an AR(3) for the differenced series.

> d. The last five values of the series are given below.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Year                  | 2013| 2014| 2015| 2016| 2017|
|:---------------------|----:|----:|----:|----:|----:|
|Population (millions) | 8.09| 8.19| 8.28| 8.37| 8.47|


:::
:::


> The estimated parameters are $c = 0.0053$, $\phi_1 = 1.64$, $\phi_2 = -1.17$, and $\phi_3 = 0.45$.
> Without using the `forecast()` function, calculate forecasts for the next three years (2018--2020).

\begin{align*}
  \hat{y}_{T+1|T} & = 0.0053 +
  8.47+
    1.64* (8.47 - 8.37)
    -1.17* (8.37 - 8.28) +

    -1.17* (8.47 - 8.37) +
